title: Victoria of Hesse-Darmstadt
sentences: Victoria of Hesse-Darmstadt, later Victoria Mountbatten, Marchioness of Milford Haven (Victoria Alberta Mathilde Marie; born 5 April 1863, died 24 September 1950), was the eldest daughter of Louis IV of Hesse-Darmstadt (1837–1892) and his first wife Princess Alice of the United Kingdom (1843–1878).
Princess Victoria's mother died while her siblings were still small children, and she assumed a kind of parental role towards them.
She married her father's cousin, Prince Louis of Battenberg, later known as Louis Mountbatten, 1st Marquess of Milford Haven.
He was an officer in the Royal Navy.
The marriage was marked by mutual affection.
They lived in many different places across Europe, wherever he was posted in connection with his service.
She often visited her royal relatives around Europe.
Within the family, Victoria was regarded as liberal, open-hearted, practical and well informed.
During the First World War, two of her sisters, who had married into the Russian imperial family, were killed by revolutionary communists.
She and her husband renounced their German titles and adopted the British-sounding surname Mountbatten, which was simply a translation of the German 'Battenberg' into English.
She was the maternal grandmother of Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, Queen Elizabeth II's husband.
Early life
Victoria was born on Easter Sunday 1863 at Windsor Castle.
On 27 April of the same year she was carried to her baptism by her grandmother, Queen Victoria.
Until Victoria was three years old, the family lived at Bessungen in Germany.
After this the family moved to the Neues Palais in Darmstadt, where Victoria shared a room with her younger sister Ella.
While Victoria lived at Bessungen she received private tuition and became interested in literature.
During the Prussian invasion of Hesse in June 1866 she was sent to England together with her sister Ella.
Here they were allowed to stay with their grandmother until hostilities ceased.
Hesse-Kassel, and parts of Hesse-Darmstadt, were incorporated into Prussia as a result of the invasion.
During the Franco-Prussian War in 1870, military hospitals were set up on the Neues Palais estate, and Victoria helped in the soup kitchen together with her mother.
On a later occasion she spoke of that cold winter, and of how she once burned her arm after hot soup was spilled over her.
Victoria's eighteen-month-old brother, 'Frittie', was diagnosed with haemophilia in 1872.
This diagnosis came as a shock to the European royal families.
Twenty years had passed since Queen Victoria gave birth to her son Prince Leopold, who was found to have haemophilia.
Now people wondered whether the bleeding disorder could be hereditary.
In May 1873 'Frittie' fell from a window and died.
This was the first of the many family tragedies Victoria would experience.
In 1878 Victoria was diagnosed with diphtheria.
Ella was moved out of their room and was the only family member who avoided the illness.
Victoria's mother nursed her and the other sick members of the family for several weeks.
Victoria's sister Marie died in 1878.
Just as the illnesses began to release their grip on the family, Victoria's mother fell ill.
She died on 14 December, the same date on which her father, Prince Albert, had died seventeen years earlier.
As Victoria was the eldest child in the sibling group, she took on a maternal role towards her younger siblings and had to support her father.
Later she wrote, 'My mother's death was a loss that could not be repaired ...
My childhood ended with her death, for I became the eldest and most responsible.'
Marriage and family
At various family gatherings Victoria had often met her father's cousin, Prince Louis of Battenberg, a member of a morganatic line of the Hessian ruling family.
Prince Louis had acquired British citizenship and served as an officer in the Royal Navy.
In the winter of 1882 they met again at Darmstadt, and they became engaged in the summer of 1883.
After a brief postponement of the wedding following the death of the Duke of Albany, Victoria married Prince Louis on 30 April 1884 in Darmstadt.
Her father did not accept that they had found each other.
He believed that Prince Louis had too little money and would deprive him of his daughter's company, as the couple would come to live in Britain.
Victoria chose to ignore her father's displeasure.
On the same day Victoria's father secretly married his mistress, Alexandrine de Kolmine, former wife of the Russian Chargé d'affaires in Darmstadt.
His marriage to a divorced commoner shocked the royals across Europe, and under pressure from both family and diplomats, Victoria's father was forced to annul his own marriage.
Over the next five years Victoria had four children:
They lived in many different houses at Chichester, Sussex, Walton-on-Thames and Schloss Heiligenberg at Jugenheim.
When Prince Louis was serving with the Mediterranean Fleet, Victoria spent some winters in Malta.
In 1887 she was diagnosed with typhoid, but after being nursed by her husband she was well enough to attend Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee in London.
Victoria was interested in science and drew a detailed geological map of Malta.
She also took part in archaeological excavations both there and in Germany.
She wrote several essays on the books she had read.
The books covered a wide range of subjects, including socialist theory.
She taught her children herself and often exposed them to new ideas and innovations.
She taught her son Louis until he was ten years old.

In 1968 he called her '[...] a walking encyclopaedia. Throughout her life she stored knowledge of all kinds of subjects, and she had the great gift of making everything she taught me interesting. She was completely methodical; we had timetables for every subject, I had to prepare and so on. She taught me to enjoy working hard and being thorough. She said what she meant and was open-hearted in a way that was rather unusual among members of the royal family. And she was also completely free of prejudice when it came to politics, skin colour or that sort of thing.'
In 1906 she flew in a Zeppelin.
Later she flew in a biplane, although it was not '[...] designed to carry passengers. We sat safely secured on a little stool while holding on to the pilot's back.'
Until 1914 Victoria regularly visited her relatives in both Germany and Russia, including her two sisters who had married into the Russian imperial family.
One sister was Ella, who had married Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich, and the other was Alix, who had married Tsar Nicholas II of Russia.
Victoria was one of those who tried to remove Alix from Rasputin's influence.
At the outbreak of war between Germany and Britain in 1914, Victoria and her daughter Louise were in Russia at Yekaterinburg.
They travelled by train and steamship to St Petersburg and from there via Tornio to Stockholm.
They later sailed from Bergen on 'the last ship' back to Britain.
Later life
Prince Louis was forced to resign his position in the Navy at the start of the First World War, as his German background was unpopular.
The couple retired to Kent House on the Isle of Wight.
This property had been given to Victoria by her aunt, Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll.
Victoria blamed the authorities for her husband's dismissal from the Navy.
She believed that '... few had much respect for or trust in the authorities'.
She had little faith in Winston Churchill, who at the time held the highest civilian post in the Navy.
She believed he was not to be trusted, as he had once borrowed a book from the library and failed to return it.
The First World War continued, and hostility between Britain and Germany increased.
As a result of this anti-German sentiment in Britain, George V renounced his German titles, and shortly afterwards, on 14 July 1917, Prince Louis and Victoria renounced theirs.
At the same time they anglicised the surname Battenberg to Mountbatten.
Three days later Louis was created a peer by the King, as Marquess of Milford Haven.
During the war Victoria's two sisters, Alix, Empress of Russia, and Ella, Grand Duchess Serge of Russia, were killed in an attack that formed part of the Russian Revolution.
In Germany her brother Ernest Louis, Grand Duke of Hesse, was deposed.
During her last visit to Russia in 1914 Victoria had travelled past the same house in Yekaterinburg where her sister Alix would later be murdered.
Alix's body was never found during Victoria's lifetime, but in January 1921, after a long journey, Victoria was able to see Ella's body in Jerusalem.
Later that year Victoria's husband died in London.
After meeting her at the Naval and Military Club in Piccadilly, he complained of feeling unwell, whereupon Victoria tried to get him to rest in a room they had hired in an annex to the club house.
She sent for a doctor, who prescribed some medicines which Victoria went out to fetch from a nearby chemist.
When she returned, Louis was dead.
As a widow, three years after the end of the war, Victoria moved into a residence at Kensington Palace.
According to her biographer, Victoria acquired 'a unifying matriarchal role among Europe's surviving royalties'.
In 1930 her eldest daughter Alice suffered a nervous breakdown and was diagnosed with schizophrenia.
In the coming decade Victoria took responsibility for the education and upbringing of her grandson Philip, whose parents had separated and whose mother had been committed to an institution.

Prince Philip once said, 'I liked my grandmother very much and she was always helpful. She was very good with children ... she had a practical approach to them. She treated them the right way, the right combination of the rational and the emotional.'
In 1937 Victoria's brother Ernest Louis died.
Some time later her sister-in-law, nephew, grandchild and two of her great-grandchildren died in a plane crash at Ostend.
Victoria's granddaughter Princess Cecilie of Greece and Denmark had married Victoria's nephew Georg Donatus of Hesse, who was Ernest Louis's son.
They and their two young sons, Louis and Alexander, all died together.
Cecilie was pregnant at the time and a stillborn child was found in the wreckage.
Cecilie's youngest child, Johanna, was not on the plane.
She was adopted by her uncle, Prince Louis of Hesse-Darmstadt, but the little girl lived only eighteen months longer than her parents and elder brothers.
She died in 1939 of meningitis.
Further tragedies struck Victoria's life after her son Georg died of cancer in 1938.
During the Second World War Victoria's residence at Kensington Palace was bombed, whereupon she moved in with George VI at Windsor Castle.
Her surviving son Louis and two of her grandchildren served in the Royal Navy, while her German relatives fought on the enemy side.
Victoria worried greatly about her children and grandchildren as the years went by.
Her daughter Alice remained in occupied Greece and had little opportunity to communicate with her mother during the four years when the war was at its most intense.
After the Allied victory, her son Louis was offered the office of Viceroy of India, but she opposed his acceptance of the offer.
She thought that this position would involve considerable danger.
Despite her displeasure, he chose to take up the post.
In the summer of 1950 Victoria contracted bronchitis, allegedly because she had smoked since she was sixteen.
She was then staying at Louis's home at Broadlands in Hampshire.
'It is better to die at home,' she said, and returned to Kensington Palace, where she died on 24 September 1950.
She was buried four days later at St Mildred's Church in Whippingham on the Isle of Wight.
Legacy
With the help of Baroness Sophie Buxhoeveden, Victoria managed to write her memoirs.
They are held in the Mountbatten Archive at the University of Southampton.
They may be an interesting source for historians specialising in royal personalities.
A selection of Queen Victoria's letters to her granddaughter Victoria has been published with commentary by Richard Hough and an introduction by Victoria's granddaughter Patricia Mountbatten.
Victoria's son remembered her as a good mother: 'My mother was very quick to learn, very talkative, very aggressive and argumentative.
With her marvellous brain she sharpened people's wits'.
Her grandchild says that she was 'formidable, but never frightening ... a thoroughly honest woman, full of common sense and modesty.'

At the end of her life Victoria wrote her own epitaph in a letter and in conversation with her son: 'What will be remembered when history is written is the good deeds done by the individual, and that has nothing to do with rank or title ... I never thought I should be known only as your mother. You are so well known now and nobody knows about me, and I would rather they did not.'
Titles and styles
Her Grand Ducal Highness Princess Victoria of Hesse-Darmstadt (1863–1884)
Her Grand Ducal Highness Princess Louis of Battenberg (1884–1917)
Lady Mountbatten (14–17 July 1917)
Marchioness of Milford Haven (1917–1921)
Dowager Marchioness of Milford Haven (1921–1950)
